label: JZ Mock E · Paper 2 · Question 1
knowledgePattern: Compare a monotonicity condition with a restricted cubic root count
solution:
Differentiate: f′(x)=3(x2−t). On [−1,1], the smallest value of x2 is 0. Thus t≤0 makes the derivative nonnegative throughout. For t<0 it is positive everywhere; for t=0, the function is x3+1, which is strictly increasing despite its zero derivative at one point. If t>0, the derivative is negative near zero, so P fails. Hence P holds exactly when t≤0.

For Q, subtract 1 and factor: x(x2−3t)=0. Zero is always a solution. If t<0 there are no further real roots. If t=0 the factors describe the same root, not three distinct solutions. If t>0, the extra roots are ±3t, and they lie in the closed interval exactly when t≤1/3.

Therefore Q holds exactly when t≤0 or t>1/3. Every parameter satisfying P satisfies Q, while t=1 satisfies Q and fails P. Thus P is sufficient but not necessary for Q: answer A.

hints.title: Check the gradient on the interval
hints.body: Differentiate f(x). Use the possible values of x2 on [−1,1] to decide when the gradient stays nonnegative.
hints.recap: The sign of the derivative determines whether the function rises or falls.
hints.pitfall: A derivative that is zero at a single point does not by itself stop a function increasing.
hints.pause: Find the parameter values allowed by P.

hints.title: Solve the stated equation
hints.body: Set f(x)=1 and factor. For each factor, check whether its real roots lie inside [−1,1].
hints.recap: Count roots only in the interval the question specifies.
hints.pitfall: Coinciding roots count once, and both interval endpoints are included.
hints.pause: Find the parameter values allowed by Q.

hints.title: Compare the two parameter sets
hints.body: Check whether every parameter allowed by P is also allowed by Q. Then test the reverse direction.
hints.recap: Sufficient and necessary are two separate implication directions.
hints.pitfall: A failed direction needs a parameter value allowed by the actual question.
hints.pause: Classify the relationship between P and Q.
